segments.text: Right now, everyone has a strong opinion about where artificial intelligence is taking us.
The optimists are promising a post-scarcity utopia, and the warriors are preparing for
the end of human agency.
Both sides are absolutely certain they know what happens next.
But history shows us that no matter how confident the experts are, the most significant outcomes
are almost always the ones nobody saw coming.
To understand why, we have to look at a true story about rats.
In 1902, the city of Hanoi had a massive problem.
They had just built a sprawling modern sewer system, and it had quickly become entirely overrun with rats.
The government devised a plan that seemed mechanically perfect.
They offered citizens a cash payment for every severed rat tail turned in.
Thousands of tails immediately poured into the collection centers.
On paper, the brilliance of the plan was obvious.
A direct economic incentive should act as a simple, effective solution to a complex problem.
Then, people started noticing something very strange.
The streets of Hanoi were suddenly filled with rats, running around perfectly fine, missing their tails.
The rat catchers had figured out a biological loophole.
Rats can live a completely normal life without that appendage.
And, more importantly, they can keep reproducing.
The hunters realized that a dead rat only pays out once.
A live rat pays forever.
They simply clipped the tails to collect the bounty and let the rats scurry back to the sewers to breed.
Some highly motivated citizens took this logic even further.
Instead of hunting through the sewers, they opened dedicated rat farms
just to cultivate a steady supply of tails.
When the government finally realized what was happening and canceled the program,
they were left with a mountain of severed tails,
but a significantly larger overall rat population than when they started.
The mechanical payment system worked exactly as designed.
People delivered tails, and the government paid them.
But, by creating a market for the tails,
the program inadvertently encouraged people to keep the actual problem alive.
Hanoi's plan was fewer rats, and the result was more rats.
This pattern of unexpected results happens across completely different disciplines.
Consider a welcome surprise, and a costly mistake.
This board highlights two modern examples where the biggest results were never the plan.
First, look at SMS text messaging.
It was originally built strictly to send short, utilitarian messages over early mobile networks.
Its creators did not expect it to be a primary feature.
Instead, young users got hold of the technology and repurposed it,
turning texting into a daily, constant way to stay in touch with each other.
On the ecology side,
Australia imported cane toads specifically to eat the beetles
that were destroying their sugar cane crops.
But the toads barely controlled the pests.
Instead, they poisoned native animals and spread rapidly across the entire country.
Whether you are writing code for a network or dropping a new species into a field,
you cannot dictate exactly how ecosystems or end-users will exploit your intervention.
Now, apply that history to artificial intelligence.
Every AI expert working today is making a firm prediction about our future.
These are smart, well-researched forecasts built on solid data from all camps.
But the most important thing AI does in your lifetime, good or bad,
is likely something nobody in any lab or think tank has even thought of yet.
That lack of foresight is not a reason to fear the technology
or panic about the changes we are seeing today.
You do not need to predict the future perfectly.
You simply need to recognize the uncertainty.
Watch how people actually adopt the tools
and build skills that will remain relevant when the forecast inevitably changes.
As this quote points out,
some of the biggest results are the ones nobody predicted.
And watching those surprises unfold is the best reason to walk into the future curious.
